d.title: Prompt injection attacks against GPT-3
d.summary: Introduces prompt injection for applications that concatenate untrusted text into GPT-3 instructions. Examples make the model ignore its task, reveal the surrounding prompt, and evade quoting or AI-based detection, illustrating why conventional input filtering and attempted instruction/data separation did not provide reliable protection.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: Discovery and Disclosure of Prompt Injections
d.summary: Records Preamble's May 2022 disclosure that natural-language input could override intended GPT-3 behavior, initially described as command injection and later called prompt injection. It supplies a dated disclosure history and points to later technical treatments of direct and indirect attacks.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: Riley Goodside (@goodside) on X
d.summary: Demonstrates that malicious text embedded in a GPT-3 translation task can instruct the model to ignore the surrounding prompt and return an attacker-selected response, an early concrete prompt-injection example.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: I don’t know how to solve prompt injection
d.summary: Argues that prompt injection lacks a reliable, testable mitigation because natural-language instructions and untrusted input share no formal syntactic boundary. Pattern filters can be bypassed, model upgrades change behavior, and even purported instruction/input separation needs evidence that it remains robust against adversarial phrasing.
d.context: A related explanation or case study linked by the source.

d.title: mkgoose (@mkualquiera) on X
d.summary: Demonstrates prompt injection against an automated remote-work bot: a tweet first elicits a marker response, then asks the model to reveal its initial instructions, showing that public user input can redirect behavior and extract the hidden prompt.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: Simon Willison (@simonw) on X
d.summary: Demonstrates a GPT-3 prompt-injection variant that overrides a translation task and asks the model to echo the complete surrounding prompt, exposing potentially proprietary or sensitive application instructions.
d.context: Earlier research cited as a basis for this technique.

d.title: Yohei (@yoheinakajima) on X
d.summary: Proposes a canary-style prompt-injection check: add an instruction expected to produce a fixed word, then treat any other output as evidence that untrusted input may have overridden the prompt. The post illustrates normal and injected cases, framing the result as a possible signal rather than a guaranteed defense.

d.title: HTTP Request Smuggling in the Multiverse of Parsing Flaws (Slides)

Cloudflare Pages, part 1: The fellowship of the secret
Cloudflare Pages, part 2: The two privescs
d.summary: Continues the Cloudflare Pages chain by injecting an Azure Pipelines logging command to control a later variable, gaining the AzDevOps user and passwordless sudo. Root access inside the build container reaches a mounted Docker socket, enabling host escape and disclosure of Azure DevOps tokens and cross-tenant build data.
d.context: The second article continues the investigation through Azure DevOps variable injection, privilege escalation and Docker-socket host escape.

d.title: Cloudflare Pages, part 3: The return of the secrets
d.summary: Tests Cloudflare Pages' rearchitected GKE and gVisor build service and finds missing network isolation between tenant pods and Kubernetes node services. Anonymous kubelet /pods responses expose Git credentials, and scanning the cluster subnet finds the endpoint on other hosts, enabling cross-tenant secret theft.
d.context: The third article evaluates the rearchitected platform and documents missing workload isolation and exposed kubelet data across tenants.
